The analytic background yields exact constraints on the spectrum. At fixed azimuthal number $m$, the frequencies $\widehatω=r_0ω$ are mirror symmetric about $\operatorname{Re}\widehatω=3πjm/2$, where $r_0$ is the throat radius and $j=J/r_0^2$ is the dimensionless angular momentum. Each multipole family depends on $m$ and $j$ only through $mj$ and three angular Chebyshev polynomials represent exactly the multipoles $L=|m|,|m|+1,|m|+2$. A conserved flux confines nonthreshold real quasinormal frequencies to the superradiant window $0<ω/(mΩ_-)<1$, where $Ω_-=3πJ/r_0^3$. For the sampled sectors $m=1,2,3$ and spins up to $j=19$, every converged frequency is damped and lies outside this window. Independent integration verifies the low-lying modes, while Kerr spectra provide a separate benchmark for the two-dimensional solver. A limiting radial equation explains why the computed mode frequencies approach the upper edge of the superradiant window with frequency offsets proportional to $(mj)^{-1/2}$ at large $mj$. A complete stability assessment requires further analysis of the unresolved scalar spectrum and of perturbations of the coupled metric-matter system.

title: Crystal and magnetic structures of MnSi in zero magnetic field: Neutron diffraction and symmetry analysis
summary: Combining high-resolution wide-angle neutron powder diffraction with magnetic-superspace symmetry analysis, we refine the crystal structure and present, to our knowledge, the first systematic refinement of cubic $P2_13$ MnSi's zero-field magnetic structure across multiple magnetic satellite families. We compare single-arm rhombohedral 3+1D and cubic four-arm 3+4D magnetic superspace-group (MSSG) descriptions with propagation vectors along $\langle111\rangle$. Simultaneous extinction of the two satellite groups around $\{100\}$ dictates a transverse circular-helix model. This suppression and refinements of 18 separately varied satellite-group intensities support this ideal limit with only one adjustable magnetic amplitude. In the ideal single-arm model with MSSG $R3.1'(0,0,g)ts$, the moment has constant magnitude 0.535(3) $μ_B$ per Mn. An explicit four-arm 3+4D cubic superspace construction presented here combines four interpenetrating helices and, for the illustrated phase choice, has moments ranging from zero to 0.874(5) $μ_B$ per Mn, with the same root-mean-square moment as the 3+1D structure. Their identical powder profiles prevent the present measurements from distinguishing them. The average crystal structure remains cubic within experimental resolution, providing structural motivation for the cubic magnetic model. The mean lattice parameter, determined with formal relative precision $σ_a/a \lesssim 10^{-5}$, exhibits nonmonotonic temperature dependence below the Néel temperature.

title: Industrial RPCVD growth of high-purity 28Si epilayers with 29Si content below 30 ppm for high-fidelity electron spin qubits
summary: Silicon quantum-dot spin qubits are among the most promising routes to large-scale quantum computation, but the residual 29Si nuclear spins in natural silicon impose a hyperfine dephasing limit that must be overcome by isotopic purification. Here, we report the epitaxial growth of high-purity 28Si on float-zone silicon using an industrial reduced-pressure chemical vapor deposition (RPCVD) system. Secondary-ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) confirms an 28Si isotopic purity of 99.997%, with the 29Si concentration below 30 ppm. Through a systematic vacuum annealing matrix (850-1150 C), combined with atomic force microscopy and SIMS, we investigate the defect-mediated decomposition of the native oxide and the injection of non-equilibrium vacancies. We identify a thermal-budget window below 950 C within which the thin-layer structure of 28Si remains intact. At 1.5 K, magnetotransport measurements reveal a peak Hall mobility of 12,858 cm^2 V^-1 s^-1 and a quantum scattering lifetime of 0.659 ps, corresponding to a single-particle level broadening of 499 micro-eV. A double quantum dot fabricated on this platform exhibits a T2* of 0.62 us, a Hahn-echo coherence time of 28.8 us, and single-qubit gate fidelities of up to 99.9% measured by randomized benchmarking. Our results establish industrial RPCVD as a promising route toward high-coherence, high-fidelity silicon spin qubits.

title: Orbital texture of valence band and interband transitions of the type-II multiferroic van der Waals NiI$_2$
summary: NiI$_2$ is a van der Waals semiconductor characterized by complex electronic and magnetic phases, holding promise towards functional applications. For this purpose, a detailed understanding of its band structure and its excitations is essential to elucidate the electronic and transport properties. We present a comprehensive description of the band structure and of the lowest valence-to-conduction band transition in bulk NiI$_2$, by means of time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy supported by first-principles calculations. We describe the orbital character of Ni and I manifolds, and identify the main momentum-resolved features of the valence band and the shallow minima of the conduction band. With this study, we provide a foundational understanding of the electronic structure of NiI$_2$ and its single-particle interband electronic excitation, a benchmark for theoretical models, and a framework for future investigations on this material.

title: Momentum-dependent phonon effects on spin-fluctuation $d$-wave pairing in bulk La$_6$Ni$_5$O$_{12}$
summary: We study the effect of electron-phonon coupling on spin-fluctuation-mediated pairing in bulk La$_6$Ni$_5$O$_{12}$. A five-layer Hubbard model treated within the random-phase approximation yields a leading $d_{x^2-y^2}$ pairing state. Two phenomenological couplings motivated by oxygen breathing modes favor $s$-wave pairing when considered alone, while their attractive scattering between opposite-sign regions of the spin-fluctuation-induced gap suppresses $d$-wave pairing. Electronic charge screening strongly reduces this suppression. Comparing the $s$- and $d$-wave pairing strengths with and without screening shows that screening shifts their boundary in favor of $d$-wave pairing. Momentum-resolved projections locate the reduction of the unfavorable scattering processes. At the representative electronic interaction, $d$-wave pairing remains dominant.

title: Giant gas permeance through a nanoporous crystalline 2D polymer
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures; includes Extended Data and Supplementary Material. For associated data and code repository see: https://github.com/DelMaestroGroup/papers-code-PolyfantripPermeance
summary: Chemical separation processes represent one of the largest contributors to industrial energy consumption, underscoring the need for the most efficient separation strategies. Many separation processes rely on selective transport through porous media. In this context, two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a promising route to atomically precise porosity beyond the reach of traditional top-down fabrication, with the potential to enhance separation performance by increasing flow. Here we report measurements of gas transport through a one-molecule-thick layer of suspended, nanoporous poly(carboxyfantrip), a 2D polymer that has identical, nanometer-sized pores that cover nearly a quarter of the surface. This combination of ultimate thinness with high areal pore density gives normalized gas flows (permeances) that approach the effusion limit, three to four orders of magnitude above gas-sieving graphene membranes. We find that gases spanning nearly two orders of magnitude in molecular weight (H$_2$, He, N$_2$, CO$_2$, and SF$_6$) obey Graham's law and approach the ideal limit of non-interacting ballistic transport, despite strong, species-dependent gas-pore interactions. Simulations reproduce the measured permeances within experimental uncertainty and provide an atomistic picture of the transport process. This work demonstrates the potential of synthetic crystalline 2D polymers for chemical separation, water filtration, and quantum sensing.

title: Overcoming speed-accuracy trade-offs with medium-sized interatomic potentials
summary: Current machine-learned interatomic potentials offer a choice between small, fast models and large, expressive networks. This study demonstrates how an intermediate potential can approach the limit of transferable accuracy at the cost of the cheapest existing formalisms. Specifically, we model He-bearing W-Ta-Hf-Cr-V-Ti alloys with an atomic cluster expansion that learns the radial components of each polynomial as independent linear transforms and embeds numerous densities with learned exponents. While (near-)training loss appears largely a function of model size, the error on a distinct validation set is close to that of leading potentials with ten times more parameters. Taking advantage of the new structure, we develop optimized implementations that run more than an order of magnitude faster than the larger models and many times faster than smaller models with equivalent polynomials. The potential is trained on systematically enumerated small structures but generalizes to point and planar defects and can be extended to even more complex chemistries. As a demonstration, we simulate radiation-damage cascades in billion-atom systems for hundreds of thousands of timesteps.

title: Ballistic transport through 3D flat bands in rhombohedral graphene in an in-plane magnetic field
summary: We explore how an in-plane magnetic field reshapes the transmitting channels of a finite slab of rhombohedral multilayer graphene and redistributes the current across its thickness. The two-terminal conductance counts these channels, while the voltage at each surface reflects the relative spectral weights of right- and left-moving states on the contacted layer. In sufficiently thick slabs or at sufficiently strong fields, the nearly flat bulk zeroth Landau level gives rise to a three-dimensional Hall effect with a plateau in the four-terminal Hall resistance.

title: Coherent Control of High-Order Lightwave Currents in Gate-Tunable Bilayer Graphene
summary: The sub-cycle acceleration of charge carriers in an electronic circuit by tailored terahertz (THz) electric-field waveforms, rather than conventional pulsed bias voltages, opens a transformative frontier for lightwave electronics operating far beyond the scaling limits of gigahertz electronic technologies. Yet gate-tunable coherent control of multi-order and non-perturbative currents has remained elusive. Here, we demonstrate lightwave control over the amplitude, phase flips, and zero-crossings of THz field-driven high-order currents by utilizing phase-locked pairs of single-cycle THz fields in a dual-gated bilayer graphene (BLG) device. By leveraging the in-situ tuning of both bandgap and charge doping, we reveal extreme THz photocurrent rectification and sub-THz-cycle current generation that are governed by a strong field-driven crossover from interband multi-photon coherence to intraband lightwave acceleration, whose competition provides an exceptional sensitivity to the THz-pulse pair drive. Our interferometric nonlinear THz photocurrent spectroscopy of sub-cycle electronic excitations accesses and controls non-perturbative, multi-quantum photocurrents, which manifest as an extreme-order THz frequency comb. Quantum-kinetic simulations map these lightwave-controlled electron trajectories, revealing that sub-THz-cycle ballistic transport underpins gate- and THz-field-driven functionality enabled by electrostatic doping and bandgap tuning within the atomically thin device architecture. The demonstrated on-demand coherent control of nonperturbative photocurrent transport regimes can be extended to a broad range of atomically thin device architectures, opening new avenues for gate- and field-programmable logic, memory, and quantum simulators in which electronic pathways are steered on sub-cycle, petahertz timescales and atomic length scales.

title: Giant magnetoresistance rectification by Néel vector dynamics
summary: We observe room-temperature giant magnetoresistance (GMR) rectification driven by Néel vector dynamics in synthetic antiferromagnets. During spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance, the out-of-phase (optical) mode makes the relative angle between the two sub-moments oscillate, producing a rectified voltage due to GMR. This component is isolated from anisotropic and spin Hall magnetoresistance contributions by its angular symmetry, with its voltages scaling linearly with microwave power. We extract a GMR coefficient of 0.18-0.20 % from the rectification, which agrees with independently measured dc magnetoresistance. Reversing the Néel vector with a dc current changes the sign of the GMR rectification voltage in a non-volatile and controlled manner.

title: Hydrogen Thermodiffusion in Tungsten: Trapped Hydrogen Distorts Heat of Transport Estimation from Total Concentration Profiles
summary:
We investigate hydrogen diffusion in tungsten under thermal gradients in the presence of trapping sites using multiscale simulations. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we find that the heat of transport, which quantifies the coupling between temperature gradients and hydrogen transport, for hydrogen in tungsten is positive (thermophobic) at lower temperatures but changes sign near $1000$ K. We investigate the origin of the heat of transport and find that harmonic transition state theory with elastic thermal-expansion corrections is insufficient to explain the observed behaviour, consistent with either a breakdown of local thermodynamic equilibrium or non-negligible anharmonic contributions.
  We further extend previous studies of hydrogen thermodiffusion by including the effect of trapping sites in both simulations and analytical models. We show that when trapped hydrogen accounts for a significant fraction of the total hydrogen concentration, the heat of transport inferred from measurements of the total concentration is dominated by the temperature dependence of the trapped hydrogen population and no longer reflects the gradient in the mobile hydrogen concentration. Consequently, experimentally measured heats of transport cannot in general be used directly in continuum-scale models that explicitly account for trapping and detrapping. In such models, the heat of transport should be based on mobile hydrogen concentrations only to avoid incorporating trapping effects twice.

title: Strain-dependent Dynamics of Interactions of Iodine-vacancy pairs in CsPbI3: A DFT and Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics Study
summary: Iodine-vacancy migration and association are important factors in the structural stability of halide perovskites. Although neighboring vacancies have been suggested to form energetically favorable pairs, their stability and reconfiguration under finite-temperature lattice deformation remain unclear. Here, we combine machine-learning molecular dynamics (MLMD) and density functional theory (DFT) to investigate neighboring iodine vacancies in tilted CsPbI3 under isotropic and biaxial strain. The MLMD trajectories reveal a nonmonotonic dependence of short-time hopping fractions on strain, with strong isotropic compression favoring point-like separation and tension promoting pair-preserving relay hopping. Notably, biaxial compression produces distinct orientation-dependent responses: vacancy pairs initially aligned with the compressed plane preferentially undergo separation, whereas those perpendicular to the plane predominantly exhibit relay hopping. Complementary static calculations using DFT and the SevenNet-0 potential yield repulsive interactions for all configurations examined. These findings highlight the importance of finite-temperature dynamics and strain-dependent local geometry in understanding vacancy-pair stability and reconfiguration in halide perovskites.

title: Frustrated Magnetism from Dimerized $S = 1/2$ Co$^{2+}$ in Rose-Phase Na$_2$CoP$_2$O$_7$
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Includes Supplementary Material. Submitted to Physical Review Materials
summary: We report the growth of high-quality single crystals and the magnetic, thermodynamic, and dielectric properties of rose-phase Na$_2$CoP$_2$O$_7$, a low-symmetry magnet in which corner-sharing Co$^{2+}$ dimers form an approximately triangular network. Magnetic measurements reveal dominant antiferromagnetic interactions and pronounced anisotropy among effective $S=1/2$ Co$^{2+}$ moments. Broad low-temperature maxima in the magnetic susceptibility and heat capacity suggest the development of short-range magnetic correlations below approximately 4 K. The large separation between the absolute Curie--Weiss temperatures and the characteristic correlation temperature indicates strong magnetic frustration arising from competing interactions within the coupled-dimer network. Applied magnetic fields suppress these anomalies and reduce the recovered magnetic entropy, suggesting further enhancement of frustration under field. A systematic magnetodielectric response closely follows the field dependence of the magnetization, indicating coupling between magnetic and dielectric degrees of freedom. The low lattice symmetry enables multiple inequivalent exchange pathways and anisotropic interactions while relaxing symmetry constraints on coupling among spin, lattice, and dielectric degrees of freedom. These results establish rose-phase Na$_2$CoP$_2$O$_7$ as a platform for exploring frustrated quantum magnetism and coupled functionalities in effective $S=1/2$ magnets.

title: Supercurrent-controlled magnon transport via suppression of the superconducting gap
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures, Accepted for publication in Physical Review Applied
summary: Understanding interactions between different low-energy excitations is a central theme in condensed-matter physics. Magnons and superconducting condensates represent two distinct macroscopic quantum states, yet their mutual interaction remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate supercurrent-controlled magnon transport in a ferromagnet/superconductor heterostructure. We observe that the magnon transport signal decreases as the supercurrent increases. This suppression originates from a supercurrent-induced reduction of the superconducting gap, which enhances magnon dissipation into the superconductor via Bogoliubov quasiparticles. Our results provide direct experimental evidence of a supercurrent-controlled interaction between magnons and quasiparticles in the superconductor. The approach used in this study relies on supercurrents, enabling magnon modulation without Joule heating. These findings establish a new route to control magnons via superconductivity and pave the way for energy-efficient magnonic devices.

title: More particles or the pair? An exact test of how to improve mode-coupling theory
summary: How a dense liquid arrests into a glass remains a central problem in physics. Mode-coupling theory (MCT), the leading microscopic theory of the glass transition, fails to reproduce mean-field caging. Two routes are proposed to repair it: tracking more-particle correlations, or enforcing repulsion within each colliding pair. Testing both on an exact benchmark liquid, we show that MCT lets touching spheres pass through each other at all orders: adding particles dilutes memory and worsens the transition, whereas restoring pair impenetrability recovers mean-field arrest and the cage size.

title: The Photonic Bath at Infinity: Foundations, Derivations, and Consistency Checks
summary: The photonic bath at infinity represents the unbounded electromagnetic environment as an effective reservoir in the nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism. It accounts for outgoing radiation and incoming electromagnetic fluctuations, allowing radiative transport to be described consistently. We clarify how environmental fluctuations are incorporated without double-counting the outgoing radiation response already contained in the free retarded Green's function. We develop four complementary approaches to deriving the bath self-energy: infinitesimal environmental absorption, semi-infinite leads, inversion of the free Green's function, and sesquilinear forms with outgoing radiation boundary conditions. In particular, we present an explicit three-site matrix inversion for a planar geometry and introduce a sesquilinear form that relates the bath self-energy to the Silver--Müller radiation condition. We establish the connections among these approaches and obtain explicit bath self-energies for one-dimensional, planar, and spherical geometries. The resulting bath self-energies reproduce the Planck spectrum, the Stefan--Boltzmann law, and radiation pressure, and provide the radiative contribution required for energy conservation in photon NEGF.

title: How Path Integral Diffusion Decides a Finite Spin Glass
summary: When an AI diffusion-type generator samples a frustrated spin glass, which macroscopic alternatives does it decide first, and when? We study this for bridge-diffusion models of the Path Integral Diffusion (PID) type started from a point source. We show that every isotropic PID is a time-changed Gaussian stochastic localization, and conversely every signal-to-noise schedule is realized by a PID protocol. What a continuous-time generator decides therefore does not depend on the protocol, which only sets when and at what cost. We describe the generator's state by its partial commitments: the probabilities it assigns, at each moment, to nested classes of configurations fixed by the target. The partial commitments are martingales that move only along class contrasts. Their ensemble average gives the information about each level at an exact rate set by squared magnetization contrasts. Each split is decided, approximately, like a binary Gaussian channel at signal-to-noise ratio 1.04/λ_P, with λ_P the leading eigenvalue of the parent's correlation matrix. The theory is applied to Bethe-lattice and Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) glasses with up to 64 spins. It is observed generically that a trajectory first shifts its weight to one of the two mirror halves of the zero-field measure and then to the glassy classes inside it. These classes appear near the glass transition and keep their identity on cooling. Nested glassy levels have similar λ_P and are decided together, so a trajectory commits in one or two distinct events---the mirror choice and a compound glassy decision---which separate further with coupling and size, as the spectra predict. For a generator that takes finitely many steps, the protocol matters through the late, local stage rather than the macroscopic decisions.

title: Computing Classical Partition Functions via Cycle-Space Sampling
summary: We present a method for computing thermodynamic properties of classical spin systems by reformulating the partition function as a sum over even subgraphs of the interaction graph. Starting from the high-temperature expansion, we show that the expansion coefficients are determined by the weight distribution of the null space of the binary incidence matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and that this statement holds verbatim for multi-spin interactions once the graph is replaced by a hypergraph. We introduce a Monte Carlo scheme based on the $1/t$ Wang-Landau algorithm that performs a random walk directly in this null space. Because the weight distribution is temperature independent, a single estimate yields the zero-field partition function, and the thermodynamic quantities obtained from its temperature derivatives, at arbitrary temperature. We validate the approach against exact finite-size results on the two-dimensional triangular-lattice Ising model, apply it to the three- and four-dimensional hypercubic Ising models where no exact solution is available, and to the two- and three-dimensional Baxter-Wu models, whose three-spin interactions place them outside the reach of Pfaffian methods. For the two-body models we compare against conventional Wang-Landau sampling in energy space; for the Baxter-Wu models we validate against exact enumeration at the smallest size in each dimension.

title: Topology to Elasticity Mapping in Thermal Glass
comment: Submitted to Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and its Applications
summary: Building on our previous work on thermal nonaffine metrics and thermal strain fields, we examine how local steric geometry controls thermally driven rearrangements in an amorphous glass-forming solid. As a structural descriptor, we employ the topological steric "theta-mismatch" order parameter, which quantifies local deviations of bond angles from the steric reference geometry and is used to distinguish low- and high-mismatch particle populations. We then compare their thermal nonaffine response, thermal deviatoric strain, and thermal volumetric strain over a broad temperature range at several state points. High-Delta-theta sites preferentially exhibit larger thermal nonaffine motion and stronger thermal deviatoric strain, particularly in the deeply jammed regime, indicating that geometrically frustrated regions are preferentially associated with localized mechanical distortions. The thermal volumetric response exhibits a distinct mismatch-dependent crossover: low-Delta-theta sites predominantly contribute to the small-strain response, whereas high-Delta-theta sites contribute more strongly to the large-strain tail. The contrast between low- and high-mismatch populations is most pronounced in the deeply jammed regime, remains identifiable through the intermediate viscoelastic regime, and progressively weakens upon heating toward the liquid state. These results establish a direct connection between local steric frustration and thermally activated mechanical response, showing that thermal nonaffine metrics and thermal strain fields provide a physically transparent bridge between local structure and thermally driven rearrangements in amorphous glasses.

title: Frank Elastic Anisotropy Induced by Anisotropic Attractive Interactions in Nematic Liquid Crystals
summary: We present a mean-field theory to calculate the Frank elastic constants of a nematic liquid crystal with an anisotropic Maier--Saupe (MS) attractive interaction restricted to a cylindrical interaction volume of height $L_z$ and diameter $L_c$. The shape of the interaction volume is characterized by the aspect ratio $α_z=L_z/L_c$, which controls the spatial anisotropy of the attractive interaction. We derive expressions for the splay $(K_{11})$, twist $(K_{22})$, and bend $(K_{33})$ elastic constants and calculate them numerically as functions of concentration and temperature. At the special aspect ratio $α_z=\sqrt{3}/2$, the transverse and axial second moments are equal, yielding the one-constant relation $K_{11}=K_{22}=K_{33}$ over the full ranges of concentration and temperature considered. Away from this point, oblate and prolate interaction volumes produce distinct elastic anisotropies. Changes in concentration or temperature can also reverse the hierarchy of the three elastic constants.

title: Magnetotropic signatures of Fulde-Ferrell Pairing in a Pauli-limited superconductor
summary: Resonant torsion magnetometry measures the angular curvature of the free energy and is sensitive to magnetic anisotropy. We calculate its response for a clean Pauli-limited superconductor with single-plane-wave Fulde-Ferrell pairing. Field rotation drives a first-order transition from the uniform condensate into the finite-momentum phase and a continuous transition into the normal state. The first-order line produces a sharp softening whose integrated weight is fixed by the magnetization jump, so the dip alone does not identify finite momentum. The distinguishing response is a broad softening inside the Fulde-Ferrell phase, caused by relaxation of the gap and pairing momentum, followed by a finite step at the upper critical field.

title: Connate Topological Superconductivity and Vortex-Position-Controlled Majorana Modes in the Intergrowth Superconductor Th$_2$Mo$_2$Ir$_2$Si$_4$C
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures; Supplemental Material included (19 pages, 14 figures)
summary: The recently synthesized intergrowth compound Th$_2$Mo$_2$Ir$_2$Si$_4$C is an experimentally established bulk superconductor whose topological electronic structure remains unexplored. Here, we identify it as a candidate for connate topological superconductivity and reveal two microscopic routes to vortex Majorana zero modes. First-principles and tight-binding-model calculations uncover Mo--Th band inversion and helical surface states enabled by interorbital spin--orbit coupling between Mo--d$_{xz/yz}$ and Th--d$_{x^2-y^2}$ orbitals. Vortex Bogoliubov--de Gennes calculations further establish a relatively robust surface-state-associated Kitaev phase and a weakly gapped, Th-orbital-derived Kitaev phase. For the latter, shifting the vortex core closes and reopens the vortex-line gap and reverses its one-dimensional topological invariant, consistent with an effective Kitaev-chain mass inversion. Finite-length-vortex calculations reveal distinct spatial and spin-resolved signatures of their Majorana end modes. The orbital Kitaev phase can also exist without helical surface states in a modified model. Although the small orbital-derived gap limits quantitative predictions of experimental observability in this compound, the uncovered mechanism suggests a route to Majorana vortices in multiorbital superconductors beyond the conventional surface-state scenario.

title: Where reconfiguration makes a structure stronger
comment: 32 pages, 9 figures, 8 supplementary figures, 1 supplementary table
summary: Mechanical metamaterials can reconfigure on command and learn, so adaptation is a central promise of the field. Can reconfiguration make a metamaterial stronger? The answer depends on the comparison. Against the best fixed design of the same mass, the advantage of reconfiguring is often exactly zero. Reconfiguring helps only if the self-stress the actuators add lowers every member at its limit simultaneously. It vanishes where a member at its limit is one no self-stress can change, which the geometry fixes, or where those members are coupled so that lowering one raises another, which depends on the geometry and the loads together. Where neither block applies the gain can be large, as in a twelve-spoke hub with its worst member utilisation reduced by 29.1%. Whether reconfiguration is worthwhile is decided by how the self-stress of a structure meets the members setting its capacity under load, and can be tested in advance.

title: Topology, geometry and fabrication of volumetric plain weaves
summary: Plain weave is one of the simplest woven structures, formed by two sets of yarns that cross at right angles in an alternating over-under pattern. While such woven fabrics are usually confined to a 2D surface, here we propose a practical approach to fabricate volumetric plain weaves, entanglements featuring three mutually orthogonal families of yarns threaded through a cubic lattice. We develop an analytic framework that converts the crossing pattern topology into continuous yarn centreline geometries, which we then leverage to fabricate volumetric weave specimens. Each crossing is encoded by a matrix that defines the offsets of the three yarns at a vertex. These are formulated to preserve the plain weave topology in every plane, where each pair of yarn families interlaces as in a planar plain weave. Eight configurations in four opposite pairs exist, yet all are related by rotations and translations, so that the fully alternating volumetric plain weave has a single topology. We adopt sinusoidal yarn trajectories and show that the crossing matrix defines their phases. We select two solutions: in-phase planar zigzags and out-of-phase circular helices. Both are members of a family of elliptical helices that also admits a free choice of handedness for each yarn. We then derive the conditions under which yarns intersect between vertices. In-phase yarns never intersect, whereas helical yarns of equal handedness intersect at a critical offset of $\sqrt{2}λ/16$, with $λ$ the wavelength of the cubic lattice. No assignment of handedness avoids these intersections. Finally, we fabricate volumetric plain weaves by 3D printing and manual assembly from cotton cord. The framework provides a direct basis for generating weave geometries for simulation and fabrication.

title: Spatial effects of Kuramoto modeling on the power-grid frequencies
summary:
Spatial coupling and heterogeneity can generate complex power-grid frequency dynamics. We investigate the contributions of spatial structure, intrinsic nonlinear dynamics, and external driving using the Kuramoto model (KM), with and without uncorrelated noise, and compare its predictions with real-grid measurements.
  We analyse one month of 100 ms frequency measurements from 16 Hungarian transmission-grid sites and simulate the KM on a 387-node transmission network and two-dimensional lattices. The measured power spectra exhibit two scaling regimes, with exponents of approximately 1.63 and 2.23. One-second frequency increments decorrelate rapidly, while correlations of their local inverse variance decay slowly, initially as a power law, $τ^{-0.26(2)}$, up to 15 minutes. A superstatistical Gaussian mixture based on measured local variances captures much of the non-Gaussian increment distribution, but not the rare extreme events.
  We also estimate the non-stationary long-time frequency autocorrelation exponent. KM simulations on low-dimensional networks exhibit algebraically decaying autocorrelations and power spectra, consistent with the measurements and the Wiener-Khinchin relation in the steady state. On the heterogeneous transmission network, partial synchronization and frequency locking produce persistent spatial patterns and multi-peaked frequency distributions. However, neither deterministic KM dynamics nor independent Gaussian driving reproduces the measured spectra and increment statistics simultaneously. Moreover, empirical frequency fluctuations are largely shared across substations, whereas simulated fluctuations mainly reflect relative node motion. These findings suggest that spatially coupled nonlinear dynamics contribute to observed frequency fluctuations alongside external driving, including 15-minute power dispatches.

title: Scaling up spin complexity in ultracold assembled molecules: association and quantum chemistry of Cr-bearing diatomics
comment: The manuscript has a main text of about 11 pages (7 figures, 5 tables), 4 appendices of 7 pages (5 figures, 4 tables) and 95 references
summary: The availability of ever more atomic elements in the ultracold regime potentially enables the extension of molecule assembly well beyond bi-alkali systems to targeted chemical species for novel quantum science and technologies. The concurrent need for single-quantum-state control and molecular constants from \emph{ab initio} calculations, especially for previously unexplored species, creates a trade-off between complexity and feasibility. Here, we address this challenge and exploit inter-isotope Feshbach spectroscopy as a tool to study three chromium-bearing diatomics ($^6$Li$^X$Cr, $^{50,52}$Cr$_2$, and $^{53}$Cr$_2$) at different levels of complexity. The extracted molecular properties, including the number of vibrational levels and the dispersion coefficients, allow us to assess quantum chemistry methods. Moreover, our understanding of atomic scattering allows us to assemble LiCr and Cr$_2$ molecules and clarify the observed association pathways with quantum state selectivity. Our results suggest unique prospects for the Li-Cr and Cr-Cr systems, and, more importantly, the experimental viability of a wider class of assembled high-spin molecules for many-body physics and precision measurements.

title: Misorientations in dislocation cell structures: Modelling and statistical analysis
summary: Dislocation pattern formation is accompanied by the emergence of lattice rotations and concomitant misorientations across dislocation walls (cell boundaries). Recent advances in mesoscopic modelling of dislocation patterns enable for the first time a systematic simulation study of this phenomenon. We present simulation results for lattice rotation and misorientation patterns in crystals with face-centered cubic and rocksalt lattice structure. Statistical analysis of the orientation changes across cell walls reveals a transition associated with a symmetry-breaking bifurcation in slip system activity: Below the bifurcation, statistical tests indicate the presence of a single population of misoriented walls whereas, above the bifurcation, two sub-populations of 'incidental' and 'geometrically necessary' dislocation walls are present. Our data analytic approach demonstrates that this distinction does not require prior image segmentation and emphasizes the statistical robustness of the distinction between two types of dislocation walls.

title: Quantum-geometry-controlled pseudogap and non-Fermi-liquid behavior
summary: The quantum metric plays an essential role in flat-band superconductivity, governing the superfluid weight and coherence length. While previous studies have primarily focused on mean-field superconducting properties, the role of quantum geometry in fluctuation phenomena remains largely unexplored, despite the importance of fluctuations in flat-band systems. To address this issue, we employ a multiorbital T-matrix approximation that retains the orbital structure of the Bloch wave functions. By analyzing models in which the quantum metric can be tuned independently of the band dispersion, we show that an enhanced quantum metric suppresses the fluctuation-induced pseudogap in both flat-band and dispersive-band systems. In dispersive-band systems, this suppression is accompanied by a crossover from non-Fermi-liquid to Fermi-liquid behavior. This spectral evolution suggests a quantum-metric-driven crossover from a BEC-like strong-coupling regime to a BCS-like weak-coupling regime. More broadly, our results establish the quantum metric as a control parameter of interaction-driven fluctuation phenomena beyond mean-field theory.

title: Phonon emission due to dc-driven electron heating in a two-dimensional electron gas containing artificial scatterers
summary: We report the observation of phonon-induced resistance oscillations (PIROs) up to order $\varepsilon_\mathrm{ph} = 8$ in a two-dimensional electron gas containing artificial scatterers, activated by electron heating due to an applied dc current which enables phonon emission. Under equilibrium conditions, only two weak PIRO maxima are detectable. The dc current simultaneously generates Hall field induced resistance oscillations (HIROs). A precise analysis of their amplitude, which is modulated by the double resonance with PIROs, dramatically enhances the visibility of the latter compared to the equilibrium case. We identify transverse acoustic phonons with a sound velocity of $s = 3.4$\,km/s as the relevant mode and analyze the oscillatory amplitude modulation in the subsonic regime ($\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dc}} < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ph}}$) within the theoretical framework of Dmitriev \textit{et al.} At the sound barrier ($\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dc}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ph}}$), where the electron drift velocity reaches the speed of sound, we observe a phase shift in the oscillatory electron-phonon interaction that independently confirms recent experimental findings.

title: Lattice Commensurability and Majorana sectors of Pfaffian--Anti-Pfaffian interfaces
summary: We study Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian non-Abelian fractional quantum anomalous Hall states in half-filled moiré lattice systems. Owing to crystal-momentum conservation modulo a reciprocal lattice vector, these lattice systems admit coupled-wire constructions of the two phases without requiring spatially varying magnetic-field-induced momentum shifts. For the resulting Pfaffian--anti-Pfaffian interface, a Umklapp process can gap the counter-propagating charge sector, while the remaining four co-propagating Majorana modes naturally group into two sectors organized by translation symmetries. Our results show that lattice commensurability qualitatively changes the coupled-wire accessibility of non-Abelian states while providing a microscopic momentum structure that directly constrains their edge and interface dynamics.

title: Plasmon excitations in monolayer stanene
summary: Monolayer stanene exhibits strong intrinsic spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and notably distinct low-energy band features involving both $Γ$ and K valleys together with strong electron-hole asymmetry among group-IV monolayers. Its plasmonic properties and external-field tunability remain largely unclarified. Here, we systematically investigate its high-energy plasmon structures and low-energy collective excitation modulated by temperature, electrostatic doping and perpendicular electric field. Calculations use a $sp^3$ tight-binding model with SOC and sublattice staggered potentials, combined with the finite-temperature multiband Lindhard function under the random-phase approximation. Besides the $π$ and $π+σ$ plasmon known in graphene/silicene, stanene supports two new high-energy plasmon branches. For low-energy plasmons, thermal excitation extends the accessible energy-momentum range while preserving high quality factors and collective coherence. Electrostatic doping yields distinct plasmon behaviors: moderate doping gives K-valley dominated intraband $\sqrt{q}$ Dirac plasmons; heavy electron doping retains $\sqrt{q}$ dispersion via Drude contributions from $Γ$ and K valleys; heavy hole doping triggers interband transitions near the $Γ$ point, producing new $σ$-$σ$ and $σ$-$σ^*$ interband plasmon modes and complex multi-branch spectra. Furthermore, the perpendicular electric field enables continuous tuning of the $\sqrt{q}$ plasmon via band reconstruction below 0.3 V/Å and induces extra plasmon modes near band-gap closure. These tunable low-energy plasmons span terahertz-to-mid-infrared frequencies, promising for nanophotonic applications.

title: Impact of multi-dot configurations on electron temperature and double quantum dot latching in gate-controlled qubit devices
summary: Many currently envisaged scalable architectures for Si/SiGe spin qubit devices utilize gate-controlled multi-dot configurations characterized by their peculiar Coulomb blockade physics. One example is the concurrent use of a single electron transistor (SET) as a charge sensor and as a reservoir for adjacent qubit quantum dots (QD). We find that the SET energy spectrum impacts pulsed gate spectroscopy of the QD when the SET simultaneously acts as the reservoir and the sensor. Then, using the qubit QD as a probe, we quantify how strongly the electron temperature of the SET depends on the applied bias. It surpasses a reference experiment by 100 $mK$ even at 50 $μV$ bias. Our results provide a strong incentive for choosing spin qubit initialization schemes which do not rely on coupling to the reservoir in such devices. Switching to a double quantum dot connected to a single reservoir, a frequent configuration for qubit readout, we finally demonstrate the tunability of the characteristic latching behavior by systematically mapping it in the few-electron stability diagram.

title: Designed atomic displacements for finite-temperature phonons from few force calculations
summary: Finite-temperature phonons are usually fitted to first-principles forces in randomly displaced supercells, and each force calculation can be expensive. We introduce special optimal thermal cells (SOTCs), in which the displacements are designed rather than drawn at random. Our design, SOTC-D, starts from a harmonic trial model. It gives every supercell phonon mode its quantum-thermal amplitude, chooses the sign of each mode so that the force constants are best determined, and pairs each configuration with its inverse so that cubic forces cancel. Updating the trial leads to the self-consistent harmonic solution. Cells that match displacement correlations instead give good thermodynamics but not better dispersions. For eleven crystals, eight force calculations reproduce the effective dispersions within 0.03-0.31 THz, and SOTC-D is the most accurate of five designs in 9 of them. After one trial update, it beats random sampling in all crystals at 4-16 calculations and two-iteration stochastic sampling (sTDEP) in all at eight (supercell basis). On model potentials, the self-consistent form needs 2-16 times fewer calculations than the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation in 13 of 14 cases. With the HSE06 hybrid functional, it is ahead of pooled sTDEP at 4-16 calculations in Si and NaCl, and it gives the thermal expansion of Al within 3% of experiment at 300K. The method has limits: in Al and Si cells of more than 100 atoms, sTDEP is more accurate beyond 4-16 calculations (not so in NaCl up to 16); for dynamically stabilized bcc Zr, the outcome depends on the seed; and above 400 K, the free-energy curvature is not resolved.

title: Topological phases and scattering protected by projective chiral symmetry
summary: The bulk-boundary correspondence states that topological properties of a bulk material guarantee the existence of protected edge modes, oftentimes associated with the attractive property of backscattering immunity. In this Letter, we consider a time reversal invariant classical system with both translation and chiral, or sublattice, symmetries. We show that when these two symmetries anti-commute, the material exhibits a topological phase protected by the same invariant as type D topological superconductors. We realize such a system experimentally and observe the existence of the associated edge modes in an acoustic network. Our measurements are in excellent agreement with theoretical predictions from discrete lattice models. Finally, we show that these edge modes are immune to backscattering for perturbations consisting in two subsequent identical defects.

title: Multichannel Phonon Interconversion Drives 90 Polarization Rotation for Stable Domain Walls in Hafnium Oxide
summary: Polarization rotation is a fundamental mechanism in ferroelectric materials, yet how such rotation arises microscopically in fluorite ferroelectrics and gives rise to distinct domain walls (DW) remains unresolved. Phonon modes offer a microscopic route to such structural transformations, as geometric orientations can modify their frequencies, dispersion relations, and vibrational eigenstates when their characteristic wavelengths become comparable to relevant physical dimensions. Here, by combining condensed phonon mode decomposition with first-principles calculations, we investigate the origin of 90 polarization rotation in the ferroelectric phase of HfO2. Using the cubic parent phase as reference, we show that polarization rotation originates from multiple symmetry equivalent phonon modes of distinct eigenstates at different wavevectors in the Brillouin zone, whose coupling and cooperative reorientation continuously evolve to generate distinct 90 Pca21 variants and switching pathways. Among the 90 variants, the lowest-energy switching pathway through the Pmn21 exhibits an energy barrier comparable to, but slightly lower than, that of the 180 polarization reversal pathway through the P42/nmc phase, indicating that 90 polarization rotation is an energetically accessible alternative switching route. We further analyze 90 DW and find that frustrated phonon modes emerge at the wall center, where the coexistence and competition of condensed modes promote local reconfiguration of the lattice distortions, contributing to the elevated DW energies. Importantly, experimental observations with STEM imaging provide direct evidence of atomic mode distortions in stable 90 DW, consistent with the theoretically identified low-energy DW. These findings provide the fundamental structural mechanism underlying 90 switching dynamics, competing domain-wall physics, and macroscopic ferroelectric behavior.

title: Defects and Structural Evolution in CrSBr: Machine-Learning Potentials for Atomistic Simulations
summary: The layered van der Waals semiconductor CrSBr combines intrinsic magnetic order with semiconducting and optical properties, making it a promising material for multifunctional electronic and photonic applications. Understanding how defects and structural transformations affect its properties under experimentally relevant conditions, however, remains challenging for first-principles simulations due to the relevant length and time scales. Here, we develop and benchmark machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for the Cr-S-Br system, enabling large-scale atomistic simulations of CrSBr with accuracy approaching that of density functional theory (DFT). The charge-aware variant qNEP achieves near-DFT accuracy in predicting lattice constants, formation enthalpies, vacancy energetics, and the anisotropic pressure response of o-CrSBr. Nudged elastic band calculations reveal that pre-existing S vacancies lower the Cr Frenkel-pair migration barrier by up to 1.1 eV, providing an atomistic mechanism for beam-induced Cr redistribution and structural transformations. Displacement threshold calculations further show that Br is the most susceptible species to electron-beam-induced displacement, identifying the relative ease of removing different atomic species. Together, these results establish a validated computational framework for investigating atomic-scale disorder and structural transformations in CrSBr, providing a basis for defect engineering in materials for future magneto-optoelectronic applications.

title: Positronium resonance of electric monopoles in quantum spin ice
summary: Quantum spin ice attracts considerable attention due to its remarkable low-energy properties, described by the effective gauge theory, which mimics the quantum electrodynamics (QED). The ``effective" QED in quantum spin ice is beyond the ``real" QED in our universe in many respects. Above all, the effective QED hosts two kinds of gapped particles, the electric monopole, in addition to the magnetic monopole. Among the two monopoles, the electric monopole is of purely quantum origin, and its character has not been well resolved. In this work, we focus on the Rokhsar Kivelson point of the quantum dimer model, as the low-energy description of the quantum XXZ model on a pyrochlore lattice, and address the excitation spectrum of the electric monopoles, by combining the quantum Monte Carlo simulation with the stochastic analytical continuation. Most strikingly, the electric monopole spectrum exhibits clear double-peak structure, corresponding to the bound states and scattering states of electric monopoles. The lower-energy peak is attributed to the exciton-like bound state of an electric monopole pair, a signal of positronium in quantum spin ice. We found that the flippable loop operator serves as a local physical observable to excite a pair of electric monopoles, implying that monopoles can be detected through lattice or optical response.

title: Tuning correlated states in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene with magnetic encapsulation
summary: Rhombohedral graphene multilayers provide a flexible platform for correlated physics associated with their flat-band electronic structure.While a variety of correlated states appear in these systems as a function of bias and electrostatic doping, promoting specific correlated flavor symmetry breaking states remains a challenge. Here we show that magnetic encapsulation by CrGeTe$_3$ achieves this in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene, by using switchable exchange couplings induced by ferromagnetic substrates. We show that correlations in rhombohedral multilayers at charge neutrality strongly renormalize the exchange proximity splitting,giving rise to collective spin modes whose character is switched by the parallel or antiparallel alignment of the encapsulation. We further show that upon doping of the flat bands, spin triplet $f$-wave superconducting solutions emerge, whose layer and spin selectivity is controlled by the magnetic encapsulation, hosting in-gap excitations at the edges. Our results establish magnetic alignment as a means to control spin symmetry breaking and unconventional superconductivity in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene.

title: Ultrafast Liquid Jet X-ray Total Scattering
summary: X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) provide the temporal resolution needed to extend total scattering and pair distribution function (PDF) analysis to investigate structural dynamics on femtosecond-to-picosecond timescales. We recently demonstrated that high-quality total scattering data and PDFs can be obtained from individual XFEL pulses; here, we take the next step towards time-resolved studies of structural dynamics in solution. Using the Materials Imaging and Dynamics (MID) instrument at the European XFEL, we obtain total scattering data up to $Q_{\max} = 16.4\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}^{-1}$ from both conventional capillary samples and, critically, from samples delivered by a liquid jet. Despite the large air and solvent backgrounds inherent to this setup, PDFs suitable for quantitative structural analysis are recovered from liquid dispersions and molecular clusters in solution. We further demonstrate pump-probe total scattering from $\mathrm{CsPbBr}_3$ nanocrystals in a liquid jet, resolving a fluence-dependent photoinduced isotropic lattice strain. Additionally, empirical potential structure refinement (EPSR) of XFEL total scattering data from an aqueous Keggin cluster reveals site-specific hydration environments and enables three-dimensional mapping of the surrounding solvent structure. Together, these advances open the door to tracking not only ultrafast structural changes in solution, but also the evolving solvent environments that govern molecular behaviour and reactivity.

title: Atomically Sharp Magnetic Domain Walls beyond Micromagnetics
summary: Atomically narrow magnetic domain walls can arise in ultrathin magnetic films, van der Waals magnets, and systems with reduced effective exchange stiffness due to competing exchange interactions. As their width approaches the atomic lattice spacing, the continuum approximation underlying micromagnetics becomes increasingly unreliable. We investigate the structure and stability of such domain walls in a one-dimensional nearest-neighbor J-K-D spin-lattice model incorporating Heisenberg exchange, uniaxial anisotropy, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI). In the absence of DMI, we demonstrate analytically a continuous transition to an atomically sharp easy-axis wall at the critical exchange-to-anisotropy ratio J/K = 3/2, characterized by the softening of a localized Hessian mode. Atomistic spin-dynamics simulations confirm this transition and reveal that fitting discrete wall profiles with the conventional micromagnetic solution, as commonly done in experimental analyses, underestimates the exchange interaction and overestimates the anisotropy. Finite DMI removes the perfectly collinear wall as a stationary configuration, replacing the transition by a smooth crossover toward a strongly localized but canted wall that approaches the collinear easy-axis configuration only asymptotically in the strong-anisotropy limit. We derive an analytical expression for the DMI-induced canting in this regime and demonstrate its strongly enhanced canting response near the critical ratio. These findings establish the limitations of micromagnetic descriptions of atomically narrow domain walls and suggest opportunities for controlling their structure through anisotropy and DMI.

title: Ultrafast Inter-Aggregate Energy Transfer Drives Efficient Charge Generation in Organic Homojunctions
summary: Y6-based homojunction organic photovoltaic devices have recently achieved exceptional power conversion efficiencies, surpassing those of conventional organic photovoltaic materials. Although unusually long exciton diffusion lengths and efficient exciton dissociation have been reported, the fundamental mechanism underlying this outstanding performance remains under debate. Here, we report that structurally distinct aggregates in Y6 thin films exhibit complementary charge-transfer (CT) characters that enable directional energy transfer and enhanced exciton delocalization. Using ultrafast spectroscopy, we identify highly efficient Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) between Y6 aggregates, with an ensemble-averaged efficiency of 65% occurring on a sub-picosecond timescale (<1 ps). This aggregate-mediated energy-transfer pathway drives long-range energy migration in Y6 thin films and accounts for the remarkable external quantum efficiencies observed in homojunction devices, even in the absence of conventional donor-acceptor bulk heterojunction morphologies and despite substantial fractions of weak-CT components. Here, using Y6 as a model non-fullerene acceptor (NFA) system, we show that structurally distinct aggregates coexisting in NFA thin films possess complementary CT characters, which are expected to enable directional energy transfer and enhanced exciton delocalization. We establish a general multi-component FRET framework that quantitatively links molecular aggregation, CT character, and excited-state dynamics in systems with multiple packing motifs. This work provides insight into the development of next-generation high-performance organic electronic materials and devices.

title: The role of preparation protocols in the Mpemba effect under time-delayed Newton cooling
summary: The Mpemba effect depends on both the relaxation dynamics and the protocol used to prepare the initial states. Here, this dependence is investigated using the time-delayed Newton cooling law, comparing protocols in which two samples are exposed to piecewise-constant bath temperatures before being placed in a common final bath. For protocols with at most two quenches and a common waiting time, exact conditions for the occurrence of the effect are derived. They rule out the Pontus protocol within this model and show that the synchronous two-reservoir protocol maximizes the effect magnitude within the class considered. The robustness of this optimum is then examined by allowing asynchronous quenches or an additional quench for one sample. Numerical optimization of these extensions identifies the synchronous two-reservoir protocol as the maximizing limit in the cases studied. This evidence motivates a conjecture that the same protocol remains optimal for more general bath histories, although that broader statement is not proved.

title: Kagome Flat Bands from Self-Assembled Water on Non-van der Waals 2D Materials
summary: The properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials are governed not only by their intrinsic electronic structure but also in particular by their surface chemistry and interactions with the environment. The surfaces of non-van der Waals (non-vdW) 2D materials are intrinsically reactive and may require chemical stabilization under realistic experimental conditions. Here, we perform a systematic first-principles study of water passivation of non-vdW 2D materials and demonstrate that molecular water adsorption is energetically and dynamically favored for a wide range of systems. Rather than dissociating, water molecules frequently remain intact and form adsorbed ordered surface overlayers. These overlayers can adopt a kagome lattice geometry, leading to the emergence of flat electronic bands directly at the valence-band edge. Analysis of the electronic structure reveals a strong intermolecular coupling between neighboring water lone pairs within this kagome topology, while the locked molecular orientations simultaneously produce an electrostatically frustrated surface potential. These findings establish water not only as a stabilizing agent but also as an active element for electronic structure engineering of non-vdW 2D surfaces.

title: Quantum Embedding from Molecular to Crystalline Environments at the Cost of a Gas-Phase Calculation
summary: We present a direct-space formulation and implementation of quantum density functional theory (DFT) embedding for molecular active subsystems embedded in frozen environments (hosts) of arbitrary dimensionality, from finite molecular hosts to extended systems. The host is computed once without the embedded molecule (the guest) and is represented only by its electron density fitted in an atom-centered auxiliary Gaussian basis together with its nuclear charges with the periodic electrostatics separated into an explicit near-field and a continuous fast-multipole far-field operator. The method allows the removal of host atoms from this representation to create vacancies or other voids without requiring a supercell creation. Analytic nuclear gradients are also implemented, enabling structural relaxation of the active subsystem. We demonstrate the versatility of the approach through applications to adsorbates on periodic surfaces and molecules embedded in bulk solvent environments. For CO on MgO(001), we show that DFT-in-DFT converges rapidly and reproduces the periodic interaction energy within 0.44 kJ/mol while reducing the cost by a factor of 27. Real-time time-dependent embedded DFT (RT-TDDFET) of methylenecyclopropene in periodic water is showcased to produce a ~0.6 eV solvatochromic blue shift, while strong-field propagation of CO2 on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) yields substrate-induced effects at the cost of a gas-phase propagation. Coupling the embedding scheme to excited-state correlated wave function theory methods such as CC2 yields a solvent shift within 0.01 eV of supermolecular CC2 references, while reducing the computational cost by over 500 times.

title: Discrete time crystals stabilized by bounded measurement noise
summary: Periodically driven clean interacting systems generically heat up, which destroys discrete time-crystalline order. Here we ask whether continuous weak measurement can stabilize such order. We study a long-range interacting spin chain whose local occupation is continuously monitored. Measurements generally induce a transition from volume-law to area-law entanglement. Yet low entanglement alone is not enough: along typical quantum trajectories, the system still reaches a featureless state with no subharmonic response. In contrast, the most-probable trajectory, obtained by suppressing measurement fluctuations, shows robust period doubling. To connect these limits, we introduce a bounded-noise protocol that restricts measurement fluctuations to a finite window. Narrow windows preserve period doubling. Intermediate windows produce coexisting time-crystalline and non-time-crystalline trajectories. Over time, trajectories leave the time-crystalline group one by one, so the order is long lived but finite. Wide windows destroy the order. Our results establish bounded measurement noise, discarding the large-deviation trajectories, as a route to time-crystalline order in clean systems. They also show that the measurement-induced area-law phase is necessary, but not sufficient, for this order.

title: Gate-tunable supercurrent switching in a three-terminal quantum dot transistor
summary: We propose and analyze a three-terminal superconducting transistor switch in which a gate-defined quantum dot region interrupts a flux-controlled loop. The output supercurrent is switched off completely when the two loop arms couple to the dot with equal tunneling strengths and half a flux quantum threads the loop. The device then operates as a symmetric SQUID at half flux. The condition follows from a single geometric factor $χ$, which reduces the three-terminal problem to an equivalent two-terminal Anderson impurity model and makes the switching mechanism independent of the Coulomb interaction, the dot level position, the total hybridization and temperature. These enter only through a prefactor and thus decide how tolerant the device is to imperfect barrier tuning. Numerical renormalization group calculations across the full coupling parameter space show that the resonance is embedded in a broad region of elevated switching ratio at intermediate hybridization $Γ\approx Δ$, while both weaker and stronger coupling reduce it to a thin isolated line. Finite temperature smooths the underlying singlet-doublet transition and lowers the supercurrent amplitude, but affects the open and closed states comparably and leaves the switching ratio largely intact. Within a zero-bandwidth two-level model, a second dot level is shown to open a leakage channel that grows as the two levels approach in energy. Raising the output barrier and the realistic presence of inter-level Coulomb repulsion, however, suppress the leakage.

title: Lattice dynamical properties and interatomic force constants of transition metal oxide perovskite superlattices
summary: In this study, we investigate the construction of efficient model potentials for perovskite heterostructures by transferring relevant dynamic quantities from bulk systems and short-period superlattices. Through first-principles calculations, we provide a comprehensive analysis and comparison of the dynamical properties of different perovskite-based superlattice structures, including (PbTiO3 )n /(SrTiO3 )m superlattices, (ATiO3 )n /(AO) 2 superlattices, and An+1 Tin O 3n+1 Ruddlesden-Popper phases, where A can be Sr, Ba, or Pb. We demonstrate that as the thickness of these structures increases, the dynamical properties of the perovskite blocks converge rapidly towards their bulk counterparts. We discuss this convergence in terms of phonon density of states in reciprocal space and inter-atomic force constants in real space. Our findings suggest a straightforward strategy for developing transferable model potentials that accurately capture the dynamics of layered oxide compounds with progressively thicker layers.

title: Deriving Tsallis Entropy from First Principles
summary: The kinetic approach for q-distribution is extended through a "bottom-up" procedure to the corresponding entropic formula. In this way, the validity of Tsallis' formula, S_q(W) = k_B ln_q(W), is established from first principles. The resulting q-entropy is additive and the zeroth law of thermodynamics is automatically satisfied because the conventional identification beta = 1/(k_B T) remains valid. Entropy, energy, and all relevant quantities for both discrete and continuous cases are evaluated using standard (linear) averages. The "bottom-up" and "top-down" approaches yield the same q-distribution for velocities. The standard results are naturally recovered in the limit q -> 1.

title: Real Topology on Symmetry-Invariant Loops Enforces Superconducting Pairing Zeros
summary: Normal-state topology can obstruct superconducting pairing and give rise to gapless nodes in the quasiparticle spectrum. However, existing pairing-obstruction mechanisms largely rely on Fermi-surface topology or global Bloch-band topology. Here, we establish a new and general mechanism: one-dimensional (1D) real topology, defined on antiunitary-symmetry-invariant loops, enforces pairing zeros without requiring Fermi-surface or global Bloch-band topology. We derive sufficient conditions and lower bounds for pairing zeros across diverse pairing channels, for both zero and finite Cooper-pair momenta. The theorems apply to systems of arbitrary spatial dimensions without requiring the pairing bands to be globally isolated. We further show that such topologically enforced pairing zeros, if isolated, necessarily carry odd vorticity and can give rise to Bogoliubov-de Gennes nodes and zero-energy boundary modes, as demonstrated in a minimal two-orbital model. Our results reshape the understanding of how normal-state topology can obstruct the superconducting order, highlight the significant role of 1D real topology beyond single-particle band phenomena, and provide a general framework for identifying candidate materials hosting nodal superconductivity.

title: Revealing laser-induced modification of weak ferromagnetism through a spin-reorientation phase transition in iron borate Fe$_3$BO$_6$
summary: In the iron oxide Fe$_3$BO$_6$ weak ferromagnetism stems from competing contributions from two-site Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMI) and from on-site anisotropies at the two $4c$ and $8d$ types of nonequivalent Fe$^{3+}$ sites. As a result, spin reorientation (SR) transition $Γ_2$ $\rightarrow$ $Γ_4$ in Fe$_3$BO$_6$ uniquely comprises 90$^\circ$ spin switching and a 35% change of weak ferromagnetic moment. We explore ultrafast kinetics of such a transition as a proxy for weak ferromagnetism contributions modified by femtosecond laser pulses. Using magneto-optical pump-probe technique we reveal that the SR transition is triggered by an abrupt decrease of the weak ferromagnetic moment in the $Γ_2$ phase, and relate it to the laser-induced modification of the DMI and anisotropy contributions to the spin canting. By tuning the pump pulse phonon energy between different optical absorption ranges, we show that laser-driven impact on spin canting possesses a nonthermal character and is achieved through the charge-transfer transitions $2p\rightarrow3d$ within Fe$^{3+}$O$^{2-}_6$ octahedra rather than by localized $3d\rightarrow3d$ transitions at Fe$^{3+}$. The decreased weak ferromagnetic moment controls the threshold and the latency of the SR transition, as well as a final state. The latter is achieved via the precessional switching to the $Γ_4$ phase activated by the laser-induced heating. Final state is found to be a coexistence of $Γ_4$ and $Γ_2$ phase with modified spin canting persisting even at hundreds of picoseconds.

title: Giant Diffusion at Flocking Transitions
summary: We simulate dynamics in two-dimensional aligning active-matter models exhibiting order-disorder transitions in the velocity field. Analysis reveals that the single-particle diffusivity, $D_s$, exhibits strong enhancements at criticality which we quantify via a finite-size scaling method. This dynamical behavior at nonequilibrium flocking transitions is fundamentally different from that at the criticality of equilibrium systems, where diffusivities either vanish or remain non-critical. Furthermore, $D_s$ exhibits pronounced finite-size effects throughout the ordered phase, which also are absent in equilibrium settings. We interpret these counterintuitive transport anomalies within the framework of a flocking theory. Our results suggest that enhanced diffusion generates effective long-range interactions. This relaxes the constraints of the Mermin-Wagner theorem that otherwise prevents order-disorder transitions in two dimensions for systems possessing continuous symmetry. These results are of much experimental relevance and have important implications in formulating quantitative theories for nonequilibrium transports.

title: Scalable operating currents in amorphous W-N/FePt superconducting rectifiers
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. S. Russo and A. Sanson contributed equally to this work
summary: We demonstrate high-efficiency, field-free superconducting diode behavior in W-N/FePt bilayers fabricated entirely by sputtering at room temperature. The devices combine amorphous W-N superconducting thin films with a 48-nm-thick FePt layer exhibiting remanent stripe-domain magnetization. We used lithographically patterned microbridges to compare W-N/FePt bilayers with single-layer W-N reference films at three nominal W-N thicknesses (18, 24, and 28 nm). The bilayers exhibit superconducting transition temperatures of approximately 4.1-4.3 K. At zero applied magnetic field, the current-voltage (I-V) characteristics exhibit pronounced nonreciprocity, controlled by the orientation of the in-plane remanent FePt magnetization relative to the transport current. The diode response is maximized for perpendicular alignment, reverses polarity upon magnetization reversal, and is strongly suppressed when the magnetization is aligned with the current. This behavior is consistent with asymmetric vortex entry and motion governed by the magnetic stray fields generated near the bridge edges. At 3 K with the remanent magnetization perpendicular to the current, increasing the W-N thickness from 18 to 28 nm widens the current interval between the dissipation thresholds for opposite polarities from about 0.3 to 1.55 mA. All three bilayers exhibit diode efficiencies of approximately 75-80% in this configuration.

title: Schottky barrier height modulation and memristive behavior in a mechanically exfoliated $MoS_2$ flake with multiple lateral electrodes
comment: To be published in Advanced Electronic Materials
summary: Van de Waals materials possess great potential as core active materials for novel electronics, optoelectronics, and sensing applications. In particular, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) and other low-dimensional materials, such as hexagonal boron nitride and binary oxides exhibit memristive behavior, making them attractive candidates as building blocks for resistive memories and neuromorphic computing devices. In this work, we investigate two-terminal lateral memristors based on mechanically exfoliated few layer $MoS_2$ flakes. We study the influence of the Schottky barrier height (SBH) as a function of the contact area. We report different SBHs from 60 meV up to 208 meV in the same $MoS_2$ flake and analyze the effect of the SBH in the memristive-like $J-V_{DS}$ curves and the observed non-volatile/volatile resistance switching. Our results highlight the importance of contact engineering to obtain different memristive properties in $MoS_2$-based devices.

title: Holonomy, Spectral Topology, and Detailed Balance in Classical and Open Quantum Systems
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Verification scripts (Wolfram Language and Python) are included as ancillary files
summary: Band topology and non-Hermitian spectral theory are now applied to mechanical metamaterials, chiral active fluids, stochastic networks, and open quantum systems. We give a tutorial synthesis organized by holonomy and by one question: what can the spectral data of a linear generator reveal about detailed balance? Three holonomies recur: the Berry phase of a band, the Burgers vector of a dislocation (the integrated torsion of the defect geometry), and the cycle affinity of a Markov network (the holonomy of the connection $\ln(W_{ij}/W_{ji})$). We rederive the Chern numbers $C_m=m(\mathrm{sgn}\,Ω+\mathrm{sgn}\,ν_o)$ of a compressible odd-viscous fluid and restate the dislocation zero-mode count of Paulose, Chen, and Vitelli as a pairing of integrated torsion with topological polarization. Our central message is that spectral topology can obstruct detailed balance but does not determine the magnitude of dissipation. Detailed balance is self-adjointness in the inner product fixed by the stationary state, so a non-real eigenvalue, an exceptional point (EP), or a nonzero point-gap winding number of a Markov generator rules it out and forces entropy production $σ>0$, with $σ\ge k_B j^2/D$ for any current, whereas a real, diagonalizable spectrum does not in general certify it. In the Hatano-Nelson ring, which is normal yet has complex spectrum, $σ$ sweeps $(0,\infty)$ at fixed winding number. EPs need a separate assessment of the dynamics: with generalized detailed balance including time-reversal parity, an EP is compatible with equilibrium only through time-reversal-odd dynamics, as at critical damping of a Langevin oscillator, whereas an EP of a system with only even variables, such as an odd elastic medium, certifies a nonequilibrium steady state; in both cases $σ$ is analytic across the EP. We propose benchtop tests for each statement.

title: Topological states in fractals through a self-similar tensor network encoding
summary: Tensor network methods have been instrumental in addressing exponentially large many-body problems. Most recently, these techniques have also been applied to single-particle tight-binding Hamiltonians, allowing observables to be evaluated on exponentially large lattices. Here, we show that the scale-separated nature of these methods allows for a natural encoding of self-similar structures, such as the Sierpiński gasket, a scale-invariant fractal with Hausdorff dimension $\log 3/\log 2 \approx 1.58$, yielding an exact and compact representation of Hamiltonians on such lattices. Using this encoding, we study a Chern insulator, the flux kagome model, confined to this fractal geometry, and develop methods to investigate its topological states within a tensor network framework. This allows us to reach much higher fractal generations than would otherwise be possible with dense-matrix methods, resolving the density of states of a deep fractal with over 100 million sites. Furthermore, the larger structures allow us to resolve topology in smaller gaps, suggesting that these methods could be instrumental in understanding the interplay between topology and non-integer dimensionality.

title: Memory in biological Lévy walks from the dynamic-entropy formalism
summary: Lévy walks are recognized by the histogram of their flight lengths, while the renewal hypothesis on which the textbook model rests, that every flight is drawn afresh, is seldom tested. We test it with the dynamic-entropy formalism. Maximizing the causal entropy of a sequence of logarithmic flight lengths at fixed lagged correlations yields a chain of continuous spins on a compact interval, whose depth, selected by the data, tells a renewal walker from a Markovian one and from one with a longer memory. With one lag the chain is exactly solvable. A duality that exchanges long and short flights locates a first-order condensation of the flights at the upper cutoff, with the logarithmic range of the flights in the role of system size, and a positive memory makes the histogram heavier-tailed than the rule that generates each flight. For groups, the same construction separates the memory of each individual from delayed interactions and from drives common to all units, which an analysis of the group average confounds, and it gives the collective speed a critical point. On open data, renewal is rejected in seven of ten conditions of Drosophila larvae and in every termite, whose memory reaches a few flights back and lowers the exponent of the histogram by more than half a unit below that of the one-step rule. Wild baboons align with where their nearest neighbors, those ahead above all, were heading 10 to 30 s earlier, and homing pigeons are coupled across their small flocks. Zebrafish T cells, a negative control, remember their own speed, but no delayed coupling between the speeds of different cells survives the controls.

title: Direct imaging of vortex lattices across fractional fillings in two-dimensional Josephson junction arrays
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, with Supplemental Material. Comments are welcome
summary: Josephson junction arrays are predicted to host a rich sequence of commensurate vortex lattices. However, direct imaging of these configurations remains limited, while transport measurements cannot resolve the underlying vortex arrangements or how order breaks down.
